claims.text: Local elastic strain fields and defect structures primarily govern the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
Local strains and defects control nucleation dynamics of the first-order magnetostructural transition.
Rapidly deposited FeMnNiGeSi forms a single-phase hexagonal structure in the as-deposited state.
The as-deposited material contains a high density of internal strains and defects.
The as-deposited material undergoes a sharp, hysteretic, first-order magnetostructural transition.
The proposed intervention is annealing at approximately 450 °C for 1 hour in argon.
The proposed annealing treatment will partially relieve internal lattice strain.
The proposed annealing treatment will reduce defect density.
Annealing at approximately 450 °C for 1 hour can avoid secondary-phase formation and significant grain growth.
Relieving strain and reducing defect density lowers the nucleation barrier for the magnetostructural transition.
A lower nucleation barrier moderates the abruptness of the transition.
Moderating transition abruptness broadens the magnetocaloric response.
Strain and defect relief reduces hysteretic energy losses during low-field magnetic cycles.
Annealed samples will have a narrower thermal hysteresis loop than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will exhibit a more gradual and broader entropy-change response over temperature.
Annealing may slightly reduce the peak entropy change.
Annealing is expected to improve overall magnetic-cooling cycling efficiency.
The predictions apply only while the hexagonal phase is retained and secondary phases are not induced.
The predictions are expected near ambient temperature under applied magnetic fields of approximately 1 T or less.
The magnitude and temperature shift of the annealing response depend sensitively on the annealing protocol and initial defect state.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes treatments that induce secondary phases, whereas the falsification rule treats emergence of secondary phases as evidence contradicting the hypothesis. Secondary-phase formation would instead place the experiment outside the stated applicability boundary and would not uniquely falsify the proposed strain/defect mechanism.
